title: Impacts of Illuminance and Correlated Color Temperature on Cognitive Performance: A VR-Lighting Study
research_question: How do different lighting conditions (light intensity and Correlated Color Temperature) influence auditory and visual memory scores and reaction times, and how are these effects moderated by architectural context and experiment time (time of day)?

participants.description: Thirty-five healthy adults (M=26.51, SD=4.31, range 19-38 years). Majority were students and researchers (n=24), with engineers (n=4) and programmers (n=3). 19 male, 15 female, 1 non-binary. Around half (48.5%) used eyeglasses or contact lenses. All reported sufficient sleep (>7 hours) and no medical problems.
participants.recruitment: Convenience sampling method (word-of-mouth and university announcements). Most participants were associated with the Vienna University of Technology.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Two virtual environments: a modern interior classroom and a meeting room (7m x 8m x 3m). Five distinct artificial lighting conditions were simulated in each environment, resulting in 10 setups. Lighting conditions varied in luminous flux (600 lm, 2400 lm, 4200 lm, corresponding to 100 lx, 400 lx, 700 lx average illuminance) and Correlated Color Temperature (2000 K, 4600 K, 7200 K). Specific conditions: Warm-Dark (2000K, 100lx), Cold-Dark (7200K, 100lx), Neutral-Moderate (4600K, 400lx), Warm-Bright (2000K, 700lx), Cold-Bright (7200K, 700lx). Participants used Meta Quest 2 head-mounted displays.

significant differences in audio task performance (BDSTs) were primarily observed during afternoon sessions
significant differences in visual memory task performance (VMTs) were more pronounced during morning sessions.

CCT emerged as a more crucial predictor than illuminance for various cognitive performance measures, including test scores and reaction times. This pattern held true for all aspects except for the BDST score

findings.quote: In the morning session, reaction time was significantly faster for Cold-Bright and Warm-Dark than Neutral-Moderate conditions, indicating quicker responses during visual memory tasks.

mechanisms: The visual system's dependence on light is crucial for efficient functioning, with well-lit environments leading to faster and more accurate visual processing.
Ample light triggers rapid chemical reactions in the retina, facilitating swift responses to stimuli.
Exposure to bright light or changes in lighting conditions can affect our circadian rhythms and alter our physiological state, which can impact our reaction time.
Poorly lit settings with reduced visibility and increased visual noise can slow reaction times, as details may be overlooked, delaying visual information processing.
Motor responses, including reaction time, result from the integration of visual information and cognitive processing.
Cognition, closely tied to visual processing, depends on light quality and availability.
Higher contrast ratio in the VMT (for bright/dark conditions improving VMT scores).
moderators: Experiment Time (time of day: morning, afternoon, evening)
implementation_implications: Architects and engineers should develop lighting designs sensitive to occupants' cognitive performance.
Further research can lead to lighting systems that promote better cognitive function and overall wellbeing.

It is crucial to incorporate factors like illuminance, CCT, and daytime conditions when designing lighting environments, especially in settings where health and cognitive performance are paramount (e.g., schools, hospitals, workplaces).
Understanding the relationship between lighting conditions and cognition can guide the design of environments for enhanced cognitive performance.
Evidence-based design methods can become more affordable and accessible as pre-construction testing methods by carefully analyzing user responses to lighting factors in virtual reality.
The method could tailor lighting settings for specific space use during the daytime based on user cognitive performance knowledge.
Combining VR with lighting offers exciting possibilities for lighting research with fully customizable environments for various user interactions.

limitations: Measurements utilized in the study have yet to be validated against real-world measurement methods, so findings should not be directly applied in real environments.
Findings are possibly limited to the sampled sub-population (mainly university students, young adults) due to convenience sampling.

The age distribution (all young adults) and proportion of participants wearing eyeglasses might differ from the general population, potentially leading to different effects of lighting conditions on task performance.
VR, while offering greater control over lighting, has a limit on the number of participants who can be tested at once, making it challenging to draw broad conclusions.
Constraint in the geographical location during data collection.
The experiment used relatively low-difficulty tasks.
